topics.summary: sein + Partizip II describes the result; werden + Partizip II describes the action.

explanation.heading: Two passives, two questions
explanation.text: The werden-passive answers what is being done: Die Tür wird geöffnet — somebody is opening it right now. The sein-passive answers what state something is in afterwards: Die Tür ist geöffnet — it is open.

explanation.heading: How it is built
explanation.text: sein in the tense you need, plus the Partizip II, with no worden. The moment worden appears you are in the werden-passive again: Das Haus ist gebaut worden is the action, Das Haus ist gebaut is the state.

explanation.heading: Why B1 needs it
explanation.text: It is mostly a recognition skill at this level — you meet it constantly in signs and instructions (Geschlossen, Reserviert) and need to hear that it reports a condition, not an event.

explanation.heading: The test that always works
explanation.text: If you can add gerade (right now) the sentence is a werden-passive; if you can add immer noch (still) it is a Zustandspassiv.

rules: Zustandspassiv = sein + Partizip II. Vorgangspassiv = werden + Partizip II.
The Zustandspassiv names a result or condition; the werden-passive names an action in progress.
There is no worden in a Zustandspassiv — worden belongs to the werden-passive perfect.
Past tense: Die Tür war geöffnet (state) against Die Tür wurde geöffnet (action).
Only verbs that describe a change of state form a useful Zustandspassiv: öffnen, schließen, reparieren, lösen.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence describes a state rather than an action?
exercises.explain: sein + Partizip II with no worden is the Zustandspassiv.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite as a Zustandspassiv — the result, not the action.
exercises.explain: werden becomes sein and the participle stays.

exercises.prompt: One word does not belong in a Zustandspassiv. Fix it.
exercises.text: Das Auto ist repariert worden, es fährt wieder.
answers: Das Auto ist repariert, es fährt wieder.
exercises.hint: The sentence is about the car's condition now.
exercises.explain: worden makes it the werden-passive perfect, which reports the repair as an event; without it the sentence reports the state.

exercises.prompt: Which tense is Das Haus war gebaut worden?
exercises.explain: war … worden is the past perfect of the action passive, not a state.

exercises.prompt: Choose the form that reports a condition.
exercises.text: Ich kann nicht rein — der Laden ___ schon geschlossen.
exercises.explain: The shop is in a closed state, so sein.

topics.summary: Many verbs demand one particular preposition, and that preposition fixes the case.

explanation.heading: The preposition is part of the verb
explanation.text: warten auf, träumen von, sich freuen auf — the preposition is not chosen by meaning, it is learned with the verb. English does the same thing (to wait FOR, to dream OF) and rarely picks the same one, which is why it has to be memorised rather than translated.

explanation.heading: The preposition sets the case
explanation.text: The list writes the case after the preposition: A for accusative, D for dative. warten auf A means auf takes the accusative here — Ich warte auf den Bus — even though auf is a two-way preposition.

explanation.heading: Asking about one
explanation.text: For a thing, the question word is wo(r)- plus the preposition: Worauf wartest du? For a person, the preposition stays separate: Auf wen wartest du? That is the same split covered under wo(r)- and da(r)-.

explanation.heading: Two prepositions at once
explanation.text: A few verbs take two: sich entschuldigen bei D für A — you apologise to somebody for something.

explanation.heading: One entry to distrust
explanation.text: The list prints glauben an D. That is an error in the source: glauben an takes the accusative — Ich glaube an dich, not *an dir. It is shown here as printed, with this warning, rather than quietly corrected.

rules: The preposition belongs to the verb and must be learned with it.
The preposition fixes the case, even for two-way prepositions: warten auf + Akkusativ.
A marks the accusative and D the dative in the list below.
Ask about a thing with wo(r)- + preposition, about a person with the preposition + wen/wem.
Some verbs govern two prepositional objects: sich entschuldigen bei jemandem für etwas.

examples.de: Ich freue mich auf die Ferien.
examples.note: sich freuen auf + Akkusativ — looking forward to something
bestehen aus + Dativ — to consist of
Sie träumt von einer langen Reise.
quoted as the list prints it — but standard German is the accusative: Ich glaube an dich.
Ich denke über das Angebot nach.
Erinnerst du dich an den Abend?
two objects: bei whom, für what

exercises.explain: sich freuen auf + Akkusativ, for something still to come.
exercises.sentence: Ich freue mich auf die Ferien.

exercises.explain: bestehen aus + Dativ — to consist of.
warten auf + Akkusativ, which is why it is den Bus and not dem Bus.

exercises.prompt: Which case does auf take after warten?
exercises.explain: The list writes warten auf A, and A marks the accusative.
träumen von + Dativ, which is why it is einer Reise.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask about the thing in Ich warte auf den Bus?
exercises.explain: A thing takes wo(r)- + the verb's own preposition; auf begins with a vowel, so wor- + auf.

exercises.text: Ich denke oft an das Angebot nach.
answers: Ich denke oft über das Angebot nach.
exercises.hint: nachdenken takes a different preposition from denken.
exercises.explain: nachdenken über A. Plain denken an A is a different verb with a different preposition.
